organizations.name: National Resistance Front (NRF)
organizations.notes: Led by Ahmad Massoud; largely Tajik, mostly from the north; best financed and most active; harassing attacks, assassinations in Kabul, Kapisa, Takhar, Herat; lost Panjshir in 2021; claims ANSF soldiers.

organizations.name: Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF)
organizations.notes: Led by Yasin Zia; launched 2022; recently ended an Eid ceasefire; attacks in Kabul, Kapisa and as far south as Kandahar; many former security personnel.

organizations.name: Afghan United Front
organizations.notes: Led by Sami Sadat with Koshal Sadat; no attacks yet; Pashtun leadership; many former commandos and special operations personnel.

organizations.name: National Resistance Council for the Salvation of Afghanistan
organizations.notes: Old-guard former warlords/mujahideen; held a summit in late 2023 that produced infighting; hosts view their time as past.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Controls Afghanistan; ran assassination campaign in final year; Doha Agreement violations; shelters al-Qaeda.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Runs training camps; killed Ahmad Shah Massoud; fought alongside Taliban in Panjshir; UN Monitoring Team says it runs a weapons depot in Panjshir.

organizations.name: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan
organizations.notes: NRF says it is fighting TTP in Afghanistan.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Mentioned in the Obama JV team analogy and as a threat Taliban supposedly keep at bay.

organizations.name: Jamiat-e Islami
organizations.notes: Party of Ahmad Shah Massoud; base of NRF support.

organizations.name: National Directorate of Security
organizations.notes: Former Afghan intelligence service; Saleh and Sami Sadat served there.

organizations.name: ANASOC
aliases: Afghan National Army Special Operations Command
organizations.notes: Special operations corps led by Sami Sadat and then Hibatullah Alizai.

organizations.name: Afghan National Security Forces
organizations.notes: Collapsed in August 2021; 70,000 killed in 20 years; many former members now in resistance.

organizations.name: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Reports al-Qaeda runs a weapons depot in Panjshir.

organizations.name: US State Department
organizations.notes: Said in 2022 it does not support armed resistance to the Taliban.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Listed among groups that will not stay in Afghanistan.

events.description: Al-Qaeda suicide bombers posing as a camera crew killed Ahmad Shah Massoud two days before 9/11.
Doha Agreement; US released prisoners including Mullah Baradar; Taliban repeatedly violated it.
NRF tried to hold Panjshir after the Afghan government collapse and was soundly defeated by the Taliban, with al-Qaeda members reportedly fighting alongside.
NRF began launching its first guerrilla attacks; AFF launched.
US State Department said it does not support armed resistance against the Taliban.
Lynn O'Donnell's Foreign Policy article about an opposition summit that produced infighting.

key_claims: The NRF, Afghan Freedom Front, and Afghan United Front are the three main resistance groups; none currently threatens Taliban control.

The NRF is the best financed, most active and best known, largely Tajik and Jamiat-e Islami-rooted, while AFF has a wider network and AUF has the most combat-capable special operations veterans and Pashtun leadership.
NRF says it is fighting not just the Taliban but also al-Qaeda and the TTP, and the UN Monitoring Team reports al-Qaeda runs a weapons depot in Panjshir.
The Taliban were backed by al-Qaeda fighters in the Panjshir battle as repayment for years of Taliban sheltering of al-Qaeda.
The old-guard warlords of the National Resistance Council for the Salvation of Afghanistan are viewed as failed and an obstacle to unity.
The resistance lacks a safe haven, state sponsor, weapons and cash; the US State Department opposes armed resistance; Tajikistan, France, India are possible supporters.
Unity among the groups, possibly through a government in exile, is the key missing ingredient.
The Taliban benefited from Pakistani and Iranian safe haven, unity, and state support, making the resistance's climb steeper.
